title: The Man Who Single-Handedly Stopped WWIII
description: On October 27, 1962, one Soviet naval officer prevented total global nuclear war with a single vote deep underwater. Here is the true story of Vasili Arkhipov. Did you know about this close call?
script: Declassified military intelligence reveals a chilling reality: for decades, history books attributed the resolution of the Cuban Missile Crisis entirely to diplomacy between John F. Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev, but the fate of human civilization actually came down to the decision of a single Soviet naval officer deep beneath the Atlantic Ocean. On October 27, 1962—known as Black Saturday—the Soviet submarine B-59 was trapped in the Sargasso Sea near the American naval blockade, surrounded by U.S. Navy destroyers. To force the submarine to surface, American ships began dropping non-lethal, signaling depth charges. However, the crew inside B-59 had been cut off from all radio communication with Moscow for days and had no way of knowing whether full-scale armed conflict had already erupted on the surface. Compounding the crisis was the nightmare environment aboard the submarine. The B-59's diesel generators were failing, the air conditioning was dead, and interior temperatures soared past 120 degrees Fahrenheit (50 degrees Celsius). High concentrations of carbon dioxide caused severe thermal exhaustion, confusion, and panic among the crew. Unbeknownst to the U.S. military, B-59 was secretly armed with a 15-kiloton nuclear-tipped torpedo—a weapon with an explosive yield roughly equivalent to the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima. Believing that World War III had already begun, Captain Valentin Savitsky ordered the nuclear torpedo to be armed and readied for launch against the American aircraft carrier USS Randolph. Under standard Soviet military protocol, launching a nuclear weapon typically required the consent of two senior command officers: the Captain and the Political Officer, Ivan Maslennikov, both of whom agreed to fire. However, because B-59 served as the flagship for a four-submarine flotilla, a third officer was present aboard: Flotilla Commander Vasili Arkhipov. Unanimous agreement among all three officers was strictly required. As shouting erupted in the suffocating control room, Arkhipov stood his ground. Despite intense psychological pressure, extreme physical distress, and accusations of cowardice from his peers, Arkhipov calmly refused to authorize the launch. He insisted that the depth charges were merely signals to force them to surface, not an active attack. He successfully persuaded Captain Savitsky to bring the submarine to the surface to re-establish communications with Moscow, where they discovered the war had not yet started. Had Arkhipov yielded, the destruction of an American aircraft carrier would have triggered an immediate, full-scale nuclear retaliation, precipitating a global thermonuclear exchange. Vasili Arkhipov quite literally saved the world.
